solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Alec Robins hit for six by former England captain

indicators.note: something hit for six is knocked all over the place, so the letters of the setter's name are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A fellow crossword setter gets thrashed by an ex-England cricket captain.
explanation.walkthrough: Alec Robins was a well-known crossword setter and author. 'Hit for six' is cricket slang for a six-run blow over the boundary, here signalling the rearrangement. Brian Close captained England's cricket team in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Close was a Yorkshire cricketer who led the national Test side in the 1960s.

clue.text: I lay claim to lots of trousers

definitions.meaning: children say '... I' to stake a claim to something first
a large amount, as in having heaps of time

explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a childish claiming call, as slang for plenty, and as a name for loose-fitting slacks.

clue.text: Marine detachment

parts.note: a marine detachment sounds like a unit of soldiers, but here it is a piece of land cut off by the sea

explanation.walkthrough: 'Marine detachment' suggests a military unit of Royal Marines; read literally it is something detached in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An island is a piece of land separated from the mainland and surrounded by water.

clue.text: Lack of success upsetting tutor on reserve

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it
in a down clue, upsetting turns the word for tutor upside down so it reads backwards

parts.note: a don is a university tutor
ice is coolness or reserve of manner

explanation.surface: An academic is upset by a failed attempt to appear cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' turns DON to NOD; 'on' puts it above ICE in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning that an attempt has failed or a request is refused.

clue.text: The dizzy quality of blondes?

parts.note: dizziness is giddiness, and blondes have fair, light-coloured hair on their heads

explanation.walkthrough: It plays on the 'dizzy blonde' stereotype: the word for giddiness, read literally, describes having a fair-haired head.
explanation.definitionFit: Giddiness or faintness is the usual meaning; literally the word describes having pale hair.

clue.text: Horse eating bit of wheat cooked

indicators.note: the horse eating something takes it inside, so a letter goes into the word for horse

parts.note: a steed is a horse

indicators.note: only a bit of the grain word is taken: its opening letter

explanation.surface: A horse munching some grain that has been cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eating' puts W, the first letter of 'wheat', inside STEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewed food has been slowly simmered in liquid, a form of cooking.

clue.text: Father's conflicting degrees

indicators.note: conflicting degrees point in opposite directions, so the first one is turned to face the other way

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A dad's academic qualifications seem to contradict one another.
explanation.walkthrough: The two degrees are the same bachelor's degree with its letters in opposite orders, which is why they 'conflict'.
explanation.definitionFit: Abba is the Aramaic word for a parent, used in the Bible and as a title for some bishops and monks.

clue.text: Card game in vehicle going to Dartmoor?

definitions.meaning: a trick-taking game where the queen of spades is the card to avoid
a police van taking prisoners; Dartmoor is a famous prison in Devon

explanation.walkthrough: Dartmoor is a high-security prison on the moors of Devon, England, so a vehicle heading there carries convicts.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both a version of hearts-style cards and slang for a van carrying prisoners.

clue.text: Edinburgh — that is where duke and earl clashed first

indicators.note: the mixed noblemen come first, before the abbreviation
the two noblemen clashed, fighting each other into disorder, so their letters are mixed

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Scotland's capital as the scene where two nobles first fought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clashed' scrambles the two titles into AULDREEK, and 'first' puts that before the abbreviation for 'that is'. 'Where' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Auld Reekie, Scots for 'Old Smoky', is the traditional nickname of the Scottish capital from its smoking chimneys.

clue.text: Man with prospects — or Aussie?

parts.note: or is the heraldic name for the colour gold
digger is an informal name for an Australian, especially a soldier

explanation.surface: A promising young man, or perhaps someone from Australia?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a conjunction but is the heraldic word for gold. 'Man with prospects' suggests a good catch; here it is a prospector, hunting for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospector searching for a precious metal is someone exploring promising claims, the mining sense of prospects.

clue.text: Jack has trouble with pen

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Jack is struggling with his writing implement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a writing tool but is an enclosure where prisoners are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen is a place of confinement, and in slang a penitentiary, a prison.

clue.text: Old transport at RADA?

parts.note: RADA is the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, where a drama teacher would be a coach of the stage

explanation.walkthrough: RADA is London's leading drama school; an acting tutor there would be a coach for the theatre, a horse-drawn vehicle by another reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse-drawn coach carrying passengers on a regular route was the old way to travel between towns.

clue.text: Party understood naval indicator

parts.note: a jolly is a party or jaunt
roger is radio-speak for message received and understood

explanation.surface: At a party someone acknowledges a ship's signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roger' is the radio reply meaning the message is understood; a jolly is British slang for an outing or party.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull-and-crossbones pirate flag flown at sea is a seagoing signal of identity.

clue.text: Sow and cat having rest disturbed

indicators.note: the rearranged rest is having the animal, holding it inside
letters that are disturbed are thrown out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A farmyard pig and a cat have their sleep interrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sow' reads as a female pig but is the verb, to spread seed. 'Disturbed' gives STER, and 'having' means it holds the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To sow seed is to broadcast or strew it over the ground.

clue.text: Special reducing dissension for circles of society

indicators.note: reducing cuts the word for dissension short, losing its final letter

parts.note: heresy is dissent from accepted belief

explanation.surface: Something special cuts down on quarrels in polite society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reducing' removes the last letter of HERESY, leaving HERES.
explanation.definitionFit: Social spheres are the circles or milieus in which people move.

clue.text: Empty list, cock!

indicators.note: an empty list is one with nothing in it, so a nought, the round zero-shaped letter, is put inside the list word

parts.note: a roster is a list of duties

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a list with nothing on it.
explanation.walkthrough: No separate word signals the insertion: 'Empty' does it alone, reading 'Empty list' as a list with nothing (O) in it, so an O goes in after the opening RO.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock is a male farmyard bird, the usual American name for a cockerel.

clue.text: Letchworth or Petersfield. Only part, and much smaller

definitions.note: the clue's sense is something much smaller than these two towns, i.e. a hamlet

indicators.note: only part of the words is used: a run of letters is taken from inside them

explanation.surface: Two English towns are compared with somewhere far tinier.
explanation.walkthrough: Letchworth (Hertfordshire) and Petersfield (Hampshire) are English market towns. The letters run across 'Letchworth or Petersfield'; the definition is elliptical, something much smaller than such towns.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorpe is an old word for a village or hamlet, far tinier than a town and surviving in English place names.

clue.text: Stevedore who reduces pay

definitions.meaning: a stevedore loads and unloads ships at the quayside
one who docks wages, cutting someone's pay

explanation.definitionFit: A dockworker handles cargo, and a person who docks wages deducts money from them.

clue.text: Profitable redundancy has had dog-kennel converted

indicators.note: a building that is converted is altered into a new form, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone laid off with a payout spends it turning a dog's kennel into something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converted' looks like a building conversion but tells you to rearrange HAS, HAD and DOG-KENNEL.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase names a large lump sum paid to someone leaving a job, so losing the post proves lucrative.

clue.text: Heroine employed at Bentley?

definitions.meaning: the gypsy title character of Bizet's opera
workers at the Bentley car company are ..., people working on cars

explanation.definitionFit: Bizet's opera is named after its gypsy title character; and staff of a motor firm are, whimsically, men of cars.

clue.text: Moron edited first edition — never again!

indicators.note: text that is edited is reworked, so these letters are reordered
only the opening letter of the word edition is used

explanation.surface: A fool messes up a first edition, and swears it will never happen again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edited' rearranges MORON to NOMOR, and 'first' takes the opening letter of 'edition'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase declares that something will not happen any more, an exclamation of finality.

clue.text: Rock's ego divided by popular twins

indicators.note: the first pieces are split apart by having the next piece put between them

parts.note: a gem is a precious stone, a rock in slang
the ego is the self, I
in means popular or fashionable

explanation.surface: A rock star's vanity is split by fame between two identical siblings.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Rock's' makes the stone and the self a single unit, which 'divided by' then splits between its M and final I.
explanation.definitionFit: Gemini is the zodiac sign of the Twins, Castor and Pollux of Greek myth.

clue.text: Angel at Ikea consuming ice-creams

indicators.note: the words are consuming the answer: it is held within their letters

explanation.surface: An angel at the Swedish furniture store eats ice-cream.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'anGEL AT Ikea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelati is the Italian plural of gelato, Italian-style frozen desserts.

clue.text: Fighter's slice of bread and butter

definitions.meaning: a fighter is a member of an army
a finger-shaped strip of buttered toast or bread for dipping into a boiled egg

explanation.walkthrough: A 'soldier' is British nursery food: a thin strip of bread and butter, dipped into a soft-boiled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: A serviceman is a fighter, and a strip of buttered bread for dunking in egg bears the same name.

clue.text: Ship's load first removed

indicators.note: the first letter of the word for the load is taken away

parts.note: cargo is the load a ship carries

explanation.surface: A vessel's freight has had its first batch unloaded.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is a link ('is' or 'has'). 'First removed' drops the C of CARGO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the vessel in which Jason and the Argonauts sailed for the Golden Fleece.

clue.text: One and the same Latin image

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
do, short for ditto, means the same

explanation.surface: A single Latin likeness, identical to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the abbreviation of ditto, used in lists to mean the same again.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a carved figure or likeness worshipped as a god.

clue.text: Small county losing leading hard workers

indicators.note: the word for the county loses its leading letter

parts.note: Hants is the short form of Hampshire, an English county

explanation.surface: A tiny shire loses its most industrious people.
explanation.walkthrough: Hants is the usual abbreviation for Hampshire, a county in southern England; 'small' signals the shortened form, and 'losing leading' removes the H.
explanation.definitionFit: These insects are proverbially industrious, toiling ceaselessly in their colonies.

clue.text: Floral setting of gorse blossoming by forest

indicators.note: gorse that is blossoming opens out into a new form, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the Forest of Arden in Warwickshire, setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: Flowering gorse beside a wood makes a pretty backdrop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blossoming' rearranges GORSE to ROSEG; 'of' and 'by' are links. ARDEN is the forest of Shakespeare's As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot planted with roses is a place where flowers are set out on show.

clue.text: 2 half sealed off

definitions.note: the clue refers to the answer at 2-down, an island

indicators.note: only the front half of the word for sealed off is kept

parts.note: hermetic means airtight, sealed off completely

explanation.surface: Half of something has been closed off.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' points to the 2-down answer, an island. HERMETIC halved gives its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Herm is one of the small Channel Islands, near Guernsey, so it is an example of the 2-down answer.

clue.text: Top-rate lines in poetry at palace

indicators.note: the first-rate letters and lines are put in the middle of the word for poetry

parts.note: verses are poetry
A1 means first-class; here written AI
L is an abbreviation for line, so LL is lines

explanation.surface: First-class verse is recited at a royal residence.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (top-rate) is written AI, letter for figure. 'At' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Versailles is the vast royal residence built by Louis XIV outside Paris.
